lessons.title: The Great American Desert and Manifest Destiny
lessons.description: How the geography of North America shaped attitudes to westward expansion and the rise of Manifest Destiny.
spec_bullets: Part 1 — The geography of North America: attitudes to the Great American Desert; the belief in Manifest Destiny.
key_content_points: Physical geography west of the Mississippi: the Great Plains, Rockies, deserts and the Pacific coast.
Why early maps labelled the Plains the 'Great American Desert' and why this attitude later changed.
The phrase 'Manifest Destiny' (John O'Sullivan, 1845) and the religious, racial and political ideas behind it.
Push factors (East coast crowding, financial panics) and pull factors (land, gold, religious freedom).
How Manifest Destiny justified later policy towards Mexico, Native nations and territory acquisition.
lessons.exam_tip_focus: Linking the idea of Manifest Destiny to specific consequences (settler movement, Native dispossession, war with Mexico) — a foundation skill the period study tests repeatedly.

lessons.title: Brigham Young and the Mormon Migration
lessons.description: Why the Mormons left Illinois, how Brigham Young led them to Utah and how the community survived in the desert.
spec_bullets: Part 1 — Why the early settlers went west and the challenges they faced: Brigham Young and the Mormons.
key_content_points: Origins of the Latter-day Saints under Joseph Smith and the persecution that drove them from New York to Ohio, Missouri and Nauvoo, Illinois.
The murder of Joseph Smith (1844) and Brigham Young's emergence as leader.
The 1846-47 trek to the Great Salt Lake Valley: route, organisation, hardships and arrival.
Settlement methods: irrigation, communal farming, ward system, planned cities.
Why the Mormons succeeded where other groups failed — leadership, unity, geographic isolation.
lessons.exam_tip_focus: Building a focused causal explanation rather than a chronological retelling — the period study's 8-mark question rewards analytical links, not narrative.

lessons.title: Pioneer Farmers, the Journey West and the Miners
lessons.description: Why pioneer farmers and miners headed west, the trails they took and the dangers they faced.
spec_bullets: Part 1 — Why the early settlers went west and the challenges they faced: the pioneer migrant farmers, the journey west; the miners.
key_content_points: Push factors driving farmers west: land hunger, the 1837 Panic, soil exhaustion in the East.
The Oregon Trail and California Trail — wagon trains, supplies, organisation, river crossings.
Hardships: disease (cholera), accidents, weather, Plains crossings; the Donner Party as case study.
The 1848 California Gold Rush: forty-niners, mining methods, boom towns, lawlessness.
Wider impacts of the rushes: Chinese immigration, environmental damage, displacement of Native peoples.
lessons.exam_tip_focus: Reaching a substantiated overall judgement on the 12-mark question — covering both bullets is the floor, weighing them is what wins the top band.

lessons.title: The Plains Indians' Way of Life
lessons.description: How the Plains nations lived: tipi, horse, buffalo, family, belief and warfare on the open Plains.
spec_bullets: Part 1 — Dealing with a different culture: the Plains Indians' way of life.
key_content_points: Different nations on the Plains: Lakota Sioux, Cheyenne, Arapaho, Comanche, Crow, Pawnee — NOT a single people.
The horse, the buffalo and nomadic life: hunting, the tipi, seasonal movement.
Band, tribe, nation; the role of chiefs, councils and warrior societies.
Spiritual beliefs: the Great Spirit, Mother Earth, vision quests, sacred sites such as the Black Hills.
Warfare conventions: counting coup, raiding, inter-tribal conflict — and how white observers misread these.
Why this way of life would clash with US ideas of property, land and progress.
lessons.exam_tip_focus: Distinguishing 'why' interpretations differ (authors, evidence, purpose) from 'how' they differ (content) — the most common confusion examiners flag on Section A.

lessons.title: Early Government Policy and the Permanent Indian Frontier
lessons.description: Early federal policy towards Native nations: removal, the Indian Frontier and why it broke down.
spec_bullets: Part 1 — Dealing with a different culture: early American Government policy towards the Plains Indians; the Permanent Indian Frontier; a changing relationship with the Plains Indians.
key_content_points: The 1830 Indian Removal Act and the Trail of Tears (1838-39) as backdrop.
The Permanent Indian Frontier (1834): line west of the Mississippi as 'Indian country' for ever.
Why the policy collapsed: Oregon and California migration, Mexican Cession (1848), gold strikes, railroads.
The Bureau of Indian Affairs and how Washington tried to manage relations from a distance.
Shift from 'separation' to 'concentration' as US expansion ate into Plains land.
lessons.exam_tip_focus: Tracking change over time — the period study expects students to explain why a policy that looked permanent in 1834 was already breaking down by the 1850s.

lessons.title: Fort Laramie 1851 and the Indian Wars 1862-1867
lessons.description: How the 1851 Fort Laramie Treaty failed and what triggered the Sand Creek Massacre and Fetterman's Trap.
spec_bullets: Part 2 — Increasing conflict on the Plains: the Fort Laramie Treaty (1851) and the failure of the policy of concentration; the Indian Wars (1862-1867): reasons for and consequences of the Wars; Sand Creek Massacre; Fetterman's Trap.
key_content_points: The 1851 Fort Laramie Treaty: which nations signed, what land each was given, what the US promised.
Why concentration failed: settler intrusion, gold strikes (Pike's Peak 1859), broken annuity payments, US never ratified terms fairly.
The 1862 Dakota War in Minnesota as opening of the Indian Wars cycle.
Sand Creek Massacre (1864): Chivington's attack on Black Kettle's camp; reaction in East and West.
Fetterman's Trap (1866): Red Cloud's War, the closing of the Bozeman Trail and the 1868 Treaty.
Consequences: collapse of trust, bigger Army on the Plains, harder line in Washington.
lessons.exam_tip_focus: Evaluating an interpretation by anchoring it in specific named events (Sand Creek, Fetterman) rather than generalising — examiners reward precise contextual knowledge.

lessons.title: North vs South: the Road to the Civil War
lessons.description: Why slavery, westward expansion and abolitionism pushed North and South toward war by 1861.
spec_bullets: Part 2 — The background to the American Civil War: differences between North and South, issues of slavery, westward expansion and free states abolitionism; breakdown of the Missouri Compromise, John Brown, the roles of Lincoln and Jefferson Davis.
key_content_points: Economic and social contrast: industrial free-labour North vs cotton-slave plantation South.
Slavery's expansion as the core fight — not slavery in the existing South, but slavery in NEW territories.
1820 Missouri Compromise and its breakdown via the Kansas-Nebraska Act (1854) and 'Bleeding Kansas'.
Abolitionism: Harriet Beecher Stowe's Uncle Tom's Cabin; the Underground Railroad; the Dred Scott decision (1857).
John Brown's raid on Harpers Ferry (1859) and Southern fears of insurrection.
Lincoln's 1860 election; Southern secession; Jefferson Davis as Confederate president; Fort Sumter (April 1861).
lessons.exam_tip_focus: Avoiding the 'Civil War was about slavery — full stop' shortcut. The historiographical consensus is that it was about slavery's EXPANSION; saying so precisely lifts answers into the top band.

lessons.title: The Civil War: Impact on Civilians
lessons.description: How the 1861-65 war reshaped life for civilians North and South — economy, society, race and gender.
spec_bullets: Part 2 — The social and economic impact of the American Civil War on civilian populations.
key_content_points: Scale of the war: ~620,000 dead, the bloodiest war in US history; mass conscription North and South.
Northern home front: industrial boom, women in factories, Greenback dollar, draft riots (NYC 1863).
Southern home front: blockade, food shortages, hyperinflation, Sherman's March to the Sea (1864).
Slavery in wartime: Emancipation Proclamation (1863), 200,000 Black soldiers in the Union Army, contraband camps.
How the war reshaped the federal state: income tax, national banks, larger federal government.
Brief survey of major turning points (Antietam, Gettysburg, Vicksburg, Appomattox 1865) — context not narrative.
lessons.exam_tip_focus: Splitting impact into social AND economic strands AND distinguishing North from South — the spec wording explicitly asks for civilians, not battles.

lessons.title: Mountain Meadows and the Mormon Question
lessons.description: The 1857 Mountain Meadows Massacre and how the United States ultimately came to terms with the Mormons.
spec_bullets: Part 2 — Coming to terms with the Mormons: the Mountain Meadow Massacre and its aftermath.
key_content_points: Tensions between Utah Territory under Brigham Young and federal authority in Washington.
The 1857-58 Utah War: Buchanan's army marches west; standoff with Mormon militia.
Mountain Meadows Massacre (Sept 1857): the killing of around 120 Arkansas emigrants by Mormon militia and allied Paiutes.
Aftermath: cover-up, the trial and execution of John D. Lee (1877), damage to Mormon-federal relations.
Federal anti-polygamy laws (1862 Morrill Act, 1882 Edmunds Act, 1890 Manifesto) — the long path to statehood (1896).
Why the Mormon question matters: shows the US wrestling with religious diversity inside its expanding empire.
lessons.exam_tip_focus: Using the Mountain Meadows case to weigh competing interpretations of Mormon-federal relations — a tight, evidence-led approach beats a sweeping moral judgement.

lessons.title: Reconstruction and the 13th Amendment
lessons.description: How Reconstruction tried to remake the South: the 13th Amendment, Civil Rights Act and Black freedom after 1865.
spec_bullets: Part 3 — The aftermath of the American Civil War: the 13th Amendment; Civil Rights Act; reconstruction in the South, 1866-1877.
key_content_points: Lincoln's assassination (April 1865) and Andrew Johnson's lenient Presidential Reconstruction.
13th Amendment (1865) abolishing slavery; 14th (1868) citizenship; 15th (1870) Black male suffrage.
1866 Civil Rights Act and the Freedmen's Bureau — schools, contracts, courts.
Black Codes in Southern states; Radical Republicans take charge (1867); Military Reconstruction.
Black political participation: ~2,000 Black officials elected, 16 in Congress.
Why Reconstruction was once called the 'tragic era' and why Eric Foner reframed it as 'America's unfinished revolution'.
lessons.exam_tip_focus: Showing the reforms had real but partial effect — the strongest answers track BOTH the legal gains AND the limits in everyday Southern life.

lessons.title: Carpetbaggers, the Klan and the End of Reconstruction
lessons.description: Carpetbaggers, scalawags, the Ku Klux Klan and how Federal-State balance ended Reconstruction by 1877.
spec_bullets: Part 3 — The aftermath of the American Civil War: carpetbaggers; the balance of Federal and State powers.
key_content_points: Carpetbaggers (Northerners moving South) and scalawags (Southern white Republicans) — the labels and the reality.
Modern historiography (Foner, Powell): many carpetbaggers were teachers, officials and investors, not corrupt opportunists.
The Ku Klux Klan, founded 1866 by Confederate veterans — terror, lynching, voter intimidation; NOT founded by carpetbaggers.
1870-71 Enforcement (Ku Klux Klan) Acts and federal prosecutions; partial federal retreat after 1874.
Compromise of 1877: Hayes-Tilden deal, federal troops withdrawn from the South, Reconstruction ends.
Rise of Jim Crow segregation and the long aftermath: how the federal-state balance tipped back toward states.
lessons.exam_tip_focus: Untangling carpetbaggers from Klan founders — a regularly confused pair. Precise definitions are the foundation of any top-band interpretation answer.

lessons.title: Homesteaders, Railroads and the Closing Frontier
lessons.description: The Homestead Act, the railroads and how cattle, wire and water reshaped the Great Plains.
spec_bullets: Part 3 — The continued settlement of the west: the Homesteaders, reasons for going west; government actions and laws; land and railroads; farming problems and solutions.
key_content_points: 1862 Homestead Act: 160 acres, five years, $18 fee — and why most homesteaders failed despite the headline.
1862 Pacific Railroad Act and the Transcontinental Railroad (completed 1869, Promontory Point).
Land grants to railroad companies and the role of railroads in advertising the West to settlers and immigrants.
Farming problems: lack of timber, lack of water, sod-busting, grasshopper plagues, prairie fires.
Solutions: John Deere's steel plough, windmills, dry farming, barbed wire (Glidden 1874), drought-resistant wheat.
The cattle industry: open range, long drives (Chisholm Trail), cowtowns, end of the open range by the 1880s.
lessons.exam_tip_focus: Refusing the Homestead Act success myth — engaging with the failure rate is what shows examiner-level understanding rather than textbook recall.

lessons.title: Little Bighorn, Wounded Knee and the End of the Frontier
lessons.description: The small reservations policy, Little Bighorn, the Dawes Act, Wounded Knee and the closing of the frontier.
spec_bullets: Part 3 — The resolution of 'the Indian problem' after 1865: the small reservations policy; attitudes to the native Americans; Battle of the Little Big Horn; The Dawes Act; Battle of Wounded Knee; the closing of the frontier and its impact on native Americans.
key_content_points: Small reservations policy after 1867 (Medicine Lodge) and 1868 (Fort Laramie); the destruction of the buffalo herds.
Black Hills gold rush (1874) and the Great Sioux War: Battle of the Little Bighorn (June 1876) — Custer's defeat.
Federal response: more troops, hunting down Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse; surrender by 1881.
1887 Dawes Act: dividing reservations into 160-acre family allotments to force assimilation; impact on tribal landholding.
The Ghost Dance movement and the Wounded Knee Massacre (Dec 1890).
1890 Census declares the frontier 'closed'; Frederick Jackson Turner's 1893 Frontier Thesis vs revisionist views (Limerick, White) emphasising Native agency and conquest, not progress.
lessons.exam_tip_focus: Reaching a substantiated overall judgement on the closing of the frontier — was it a national achievement, a tragedy or both? The 12-mark band only opens for answers that take a position.

teaching_brief.option_focus: A 55-year domestic narrative of westward expansion and the consolidation of the United States as a nation. The story runs across three intertwined strands: settlers (Mormons, pioneers, miners, homesteaders), the Plains nations (their way of life and dispossession through treaties, war and policy), and the Civil War with its long aftermath in Reconstruction. Students should be able to track change over time within each strand AND see how the strands collide — for example how the railroads (consolidation strand) accelerated the destruction of the buffalo (Plains strand) and shaped the post-war federal state (Reconstruction strand).

common_misconceptions_option_specific.misconception: Students refer to 'the Plains Indians' or 'the Sioux' as if all Native Plains peoples were a single nation with a single relationship to the US Government. In reality the Lakota Sioux, Cheyenne, Arapaho, Comanche, Crow and Pawnee had distinct languages, leaderships and very different relationships with the US — the Crow scouted FOR Custer at Little Bighorn.
common_misconceptions_option_specific.source: Richard White, The Middle Ground (Cambridge, 1991); Pekka Hämäläinen, The Comanche Empire (Yale, 2008) on inter-tribal politics on the Plains.

common_misconceptions_option_specific.topic: The Civil War 'was about slavery — full stop'
common_misconceptions_option_specific.misconception: Students collapse the cause of the war into a single sentence about slavery. The historiographical consensus is sharper: the proximate cause was disagreement over slavery's EXPANSION into new western territories, not slavery's existence in the South. Saying so precisely is what separates a B-grade answer from an A-grade one.
common_misconceptions_option_specific.source: James M. McPherson, Battle Cry of Freedom (OUP, 1988); Bordewich, 'House Divided'; Adam Rothman, Slavery, the Civil War and Reconstruction (OUP).

common_misconceptions_option_specific.misconception: Students conflate carpetbaggers (Northern Republicans who came South after 1865) with the Ku Klux Klan (founded by ex-Confederate veterans in 1866 and aimed AT carpetbaggers and Black Republicans). The carpetbaggers were the Klan's targets, not its founders.
common_misconceptions_option_specific.source: Eric Foner, Reconstruction: America's Unfinished Revolution, 1863-1877 (Harper & Row, 1988); Tunnell, Edge of the Sword (LSU, 2001).

common_misconceptions_option_specific.misconception: Students treat the Homestead Act as a triumphant land giveaway. In reality a majority of homestead claims failed: drought, debt, isolation, plagues and railroad land-pricing meant most 160-acre families either sold up or starved out within five years. The Act was significant, but its success rate was low.
common_misconceptions_option_specific.source: Sherraden, 'The Homestead Act: A Major Asset-Building Policy' in Inclusion in the American Dream (OUP); Cambridge Journal of Economic History overview.

common_misconceptions_option_specific.topic: Manifest Destiny meant 'the West was empty'
common_misconceptions_option_specific.misconception: Students inherit a textbook idea that Manifest Destiny was about 'filling empty land'. The Great Plains were already home to hundreds of thousands of people in dozens of nations — the doctrine's role was to legitimise dispossession, not to describe a vacuum.
common_misconceptions_option_specific.source: Patricia Nelson Limerick, The Legacy of Conquest (Norton, 1987) on the 'Unbroken Past' of conquest.

examiner_signals_option_specific.signal: On 'Why Interpretations Differ' (4 marks) for this option, top answers focus on authors' purposes (e.g. one historian writing for a tribal-history project, another for a settler-descended audience) and time of writing (Turner-era triumphalism vs late-20th-century revisionism), NOT on what each interpretation says.
examiner_signals_option_specific.source: AQA principal examiner reports on 8145 Paper 1 Section A interpretation questions.

examiner_signals_option_specific.signal: On the 12-mark bullet-format essay for this option, the highest band rewards a substantiated overall judgement — for example 'the Civil War mattered MORE for civilian Southern society than for Northern industry, because…'. Answers that simply cover both bullets without weighing them are capped below the top band.
examiner_signals_option_specific.source: AQA scheme of assessment 4.4.1 and AQA principal examiner commentary on Paper 1 Section A 12-mark questions.

examiner_signals_option_specific.signal: Specialist historical vocabulary for this option (annuity, allotment, sod-buster, dry farming, scalawag, carpetbagger, Redeemer, freedman, contraband, Ghost Dance) is rewarded under SPaG. Avoiding these terms caps students at the threshold band even if their argument is otherwise strong.
examiner_signals_option_specific.source: AQA spec section 4.4.3 SPaG performance descriptors.

examiner_signals_option_specific.signal: Examiner reports flag the 'narrative chronology' problem on this option specifically — students retell the Civil War or the Indian Wars in date order without causal links. The 8-mark Explain Effects question is built to punish this.
examiner_signals_option_specific.source: OUP Education blog summary of AQA GCSE History examiner reports; AQA principal examiner reports on Paper 1 narrative-chronology issues.

key_dates_anchors: 1847 — Mormons reach the Salt Lake Valley
1862 — Homestead Act and Pacific Railroad Act
1866 — Ku Klux Klan founded; Fetterman's Trap
1890 — Wounded Knee Massacre; frontier declared closed
thread_lines_through_unit: Manifest Destiny → settlers → Plains conflict → reservations → Wounded Knee: the long arc of dispossession.
Sectional differences → slavery's expansion → Civil War → Reconstruction → Compromise of 1877: the political consolidation of the Union.
Mormons → pioneers → miners → homesteaders → cowboys: the changing settler experience as the frontier closes.
Federal vs state power: from the Permanent Indian Frontier (1834) through the Civil War to Reconstruction's collapse in 1877.
historiography_notes: Frederick Jackson Turner's 1893 Frontier Thesis cast the West as the engine of American democracy — a view dominant for most of the 20th century.
Patricia Nelson Limerick (The Legacy of Conquest, 1987) reframed the West as a story of conquest, race and unfinished business rather than progress.
Richard White's work, including The Middle Ground, foregrounds Native agency and accommodation rather than treating Native peoples only as victims of an inevitable march.

Eric Foner (Reconstruction: America's Unfinished Revolution, 1988) overturned the 'tragic era' view of carpetbaggers and Reconstruction, emphasising Black political agency and the genuine reforms of 1865-77.
Use these schools as flavour for the 'Why Interpretations Differ' question — students do NOT need to name the historians, but the IDEAS behind the differing views are valuable.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Brigham Young
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Mormon leader who led the migration to Utah and built Deseret.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Joseph Smith
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Founder of the Latter-day Saint movement, killed 1844.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: John O'Sullivan
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Editor who coined 'Manifest Destiny' in 1845.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Red Cloud
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Lakota war leader; victorious in Red Cloud's War (1866-68).

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Sitting Bull
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Hunkpapa Lakota holy man; spiritual leader at Little Bighorn.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Crazy Horse
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Oglala Lakota war leader; led the charge at Little Bighorn.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Black Kettle
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Cheyenne peace chief; survived Sand Creek (1864), killed at Washita (1868).

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Colonel John Chivington
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Commander at the Sand Creek Massacre (1864).

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Captain William Fetterman
key_individuals_and_groups.role: US officer killed with all 80 of his men in Fetterman's Trap (1866).

key_individuals_and_groups.name: George Armstrong Custer
key_individuals_and_groups.role: US cavalry commander killed at Little Bighorn (1876).

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Abraham Lincoln
key_individuals_and_groups.role: 16th US President; led the Union through the Civil War; assassinated 1865.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Jefferson Davis
key_individuals_and_groups.role: President of the Confederate States of America, 1861-65.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: John Brown
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Abolitionist whose 1859 raid on Harpers Ferry deepened North-South tension.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Harriet Beecher Stowe
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Author of Uncle Tom's Cabin (1852); shaped Northern abolitionist opinion.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Ulysses S. Grant
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Union commanding general; later 18th US President during Reconstruction.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Robert E. Lee
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Confederate commanding general; surrendered at Appomattox (1865).

key_individuals_and_groups.name: William Tecumseh Sherman
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Union general whose 1864 March to the Sea broke the Confederate home front.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Andrew Johnson
key_individuals_and_groups.role: 17th US President; lenient Presidential Reconstruction; impeached 1868.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Thaddeus Stevens
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Radical Republican leader who pushed Congressional Reconstruction.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Frederick Douglass
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Formerly enslaved abolitionist and statesman; advocate for Black suffrage.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Hiram Revels
key_individuals_and_groups.role: First Black US Senator (Mississippi, 1870).

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Nathan Bedford Forrest
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Confederate general and first Grand Wizard of the Ku Klux Klan.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Rutherford B. Hayes
key_individuals_and_groups.role: 19th US President; the 1877 Compromise ended Reconstruction during his term.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: John D. Lee
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Mormon militia leader executed in 1877 for the Mountain Meadows Massacre.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: John Deere
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Inventor of the steel plough that broke the Plains sod.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Joseph Glidden
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Patented barbed wire (1874), ending the open range.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Senator Henry Dawes
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Author of the 1887 Dawes Act dividing reservations into family allotments.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Wovoka
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Paiute prophet whose Ghost Dance vision spread to the Lakota in 1890.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Frederick Jackson Turner
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Historian whose 1893 Frontier Thesis shaped a century of writing about the West.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: The Lakota Sioux
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Largest Plains nation; central to the Indian Wars and Wounded Knee.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: The Cheyenne and Arapaho
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Allied Plains nations; victims of Sand Creek and partners in many later treaties.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: The Comanche
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Southern Plains horse power; their 19th-century empire fell in the Red River War (1874-75).

key_individuals_and_groups.name: The Crow and Pawnee
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Plains nations who often scouted for the US Army against their Lakota and Cheyenne rivals.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Carpetbaggers
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Northern Republicans (teachers, officials, investors) who moved South after 1865.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Scalawags
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Southern white Republicans who supported Reconstruction.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Freedmen
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Formerly enslaved African Americans, around 4 million in 1865.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: The Ku Klux Klan
key_individuals_and_groups.role: White supremacist terror group founded 1866 by Confederate veterans.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Homesteaders
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Farming families who claimed 160-acre plots under the 1862 Homestead Act.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: The Mormons (Latter-day Saints)
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Religious community who built Deseret/Utah under Brigham Young.
